runs.question: According to FDA Food Code 2026 sections 2-201.12(A)(1) and 2-201.13(A)(1), what must the person in charge do when a food employee has vomiting or diarrhea from no known noninfectious condition, and when may that employee be reinstated?
runs.final_output: Under FDA Food Code 2026 § 2-201.12(A)(1), the person in charge must exclude a food employee from the food establishment if the employee is symptomatic with vomiting or diarrhea, except when the symptom is from a noninfectious condition [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0059::c00]. Therefore, if the employee has vomiting or diarrhea and there is no known noninfectious condition, the person in charge must exclude the employee. Under § 2-201.13(A)(1), the employee may be reinstated if the employee is asymptomatic for at least 24 hours, or if the employee provides the person in charge with written medical documentation from a health practitioner stating that the symptom is from a noninfectious condition [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0061::c00].

claims.claim: FDA Food Code 2026 § 2-201.12(A)(1) requires the person in charge to exclude a food employee who is symptomatic with vomiting or diarrhea, except when the symptom is from a noninfectious condition.
If a food employee has vomiting or diarrhea and no known noninfectious condition, the person in charge must exclude the employee.
FDA Food Code 2026 § 2-201.13(A)(1) allows reinstatement of an employee excluded under § 2-201.12(A)(1) if the employee is asymptomatic for at least 24 hours.

FDA Food Code 2026 § 2-201.13(A)(1) also allows reinstatement if the employee provides written medical documentation from a health practitioner stating that the symptom is from a noninfectious condition.

runs.question: In the Utah Risk Factor Study, which four inspection line items were more likely to be violations in summer, what were their rate ratios, and what limitations constrain interpretation of those findings?
runs.final_output:
The Utah Risk Factor Study defined summer as June, July, and August and compared line-item violation rates between summer and non-summer months using rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0003::c02]. Given that a violation occurred during an inspection, four line items were more likely to be marked as violations in summer than in non-summer months, and no line items were more likely in non-summer months [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0004::c00].

The four line items and their summer rate ratios were:
1. Line 22, Proper cold holding temperatures: rate ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.23 to 1.52, p < 0.005 [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0004::c01].
2. Line 28, Toxic substances properly identified, stored, and used: rate ratio 1.15, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.28, p < 0.025 [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0004::c01].
3. Line 33, Proper cooling methods used; adequate equipment for temperature control: rate ratio 1.50, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.86, p < 0.005 [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0004::c01].
4. Line 36, Thermometers provided and accurate: rate ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.45, p < 0.025 [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0004::c01].

Interpretation is constrained by several limitations. Data were voluntary and covered approximately 85% of Utah's population in 2016 [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0002::c01]. Only seven of 13 local health departments volunteered data, and the labor of sending, collating, and scanning paper records likely limited participation [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0004::c02]. The analysis used only a single year of inspection data, which may not represent larger trends [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0005::c02]. It measured only the frequency of violations marked on inspection forms and could not determine the precise reasons line items were marked [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0005::c02]. Most participating departments used forms based on the 2009 food code rather than the 2013 FDA form, requiring line-number translation and potentially affecting apparent marking frequencies [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0005::c01]. For lines 28 and 36, the study states that more data are needed before formulating a rationale, and line 36 may reflect inspectors checking thermometers more often because of increased temperature violations [utah-risk-factor-study-2016-2017.pdf::p0006::c03].

runs.final_output: Under FDA Food Code 2026, the employee must report the vomiting to the person in charge, and the person in charge must exclude the employee from the food establishment because the employee is symptomatic with vomiting and the scenario provides no known noninfectious condition [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0058::c01] [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0059::c00]. The employee must also comply with the exclusion [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0058::c02]. Because the facility is a nursing home, it is a highly susceptible population setting, where employee illness standards are stricter and symptomatic employees are not tolerated in food preparation areas [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0419::c00] [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0667::c01]. If the employee remains undiagnosed, the earliest return condition is that the employee has been asymptomatic for at least 24 hours, or the employee provides written medical documentation from a health practitioner stating that the vomiting is from a noninfectious condition [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0061::c00] [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0388::c00]. Since no noninfectious condition is known, the earliest return is at least 24 hours after symptoms resolve. Regulatory authority approval is not needed to return if the employee was not diagnosed [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0388::c00]. If norovirus were later diagnosed, a nursing-home employee would remain excluded until regulatory authority approval is obtained and either medical clearance or written documentation of freedom from norovirus is provided, or more than 48 hours have passed since the employee became asymptomatic [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0391::c01] [fda-food-code-2026.pdf::p0063::c01]. Possible norovirus transmission is a concern because norovirus is a leading cause of foodborne illness, has a very low infective dose, is shed at high levels, and causes frequent vomiting [fda-bad-bug-book-second-edition.pdf::p0169::c00]. claims.claim: The employee must report vomiting to the person in charge, and the person in charge must exclude the employee from the food establishment because vomiting is symptomatic and no noninfectious condition is known.
The employee must comply with the exclusion.
A nursing home is a highly susceptible population setting with stricter employee illness standards and zero tolerance for symptomatic employees in food preparation areas.
If undiagnosed, the employee may return after being asymptomatic for at least 24 hours or with written medical documentation that the symptom is from a noninfectious condition.
Because no noninfectious condition is known, the earliest return is at least 24 hours after symptoms resolve.
Regulatory authority approval is not needed to return if the employee was not diagnosed.

If norovirus were later diagnosed, a nursing-home employee would remain excluded until regulatory authority approval plus medical clearance or freedom-from-infection documentation, or more than 48 hours after becoming asymptomatic.
Norovirus is a leading cause of foodborne illness, has a very low infective dose, is shed at high levels, and causes frequent vomiting.

Foodborne norovirus illnesses are linked to ready-to-eat foods contaminated by food workers, salad ingredients are commonly implicated, and any ready-to-eat food handled by ill food workers may be contaminated.
Norovirus transmission can occur through the fecal-oral route or vomit, and secondary transmission is common due to high viral shedding.

Norovirus is environmentally hardy, spreads easily through person-to-person contact and contaminated surfaces, is especially concerning in nursing homes, is not reliably controlled by alcohol-based hand gels or common antibacterial disinfectants, and may continue to be shed after symptoms resolve.
